title: User search with literal LIKE matching, and an all-or-nothing bulk import
problem: Implement two functions in users.py. find_users searches usernames for a substring, where %, _ and backslash typed by the user must match themselves, and returns User dataclass objects. add_users imports many users with executemany in one transaction: all rows or none.
requirements: Edit only users.py; keep the User dataclass as it is
find_users returns a list of User objects ordered by username
find_users matches the text anywhere in the username, ignoring ASCII case; %, _ and \ in the text match only themselves; empty text matches everyone
The search text is passed as a parameter (placeholder), never pasted into SQL
add_users inserts every (username, created_at) pair with executemany and returns the number inserted
add_users accepts any iterable, including a generator
add_users is all or nothing, leaves no transaction open, and lets the error reach the caller
contract: find_users(conn, text: str) -> list[User]; add_users(conn, rows: Iterable[tuple[str, str]]) -> int
expectedBehavior: find_users(conn, 'an') returns [User(1, 'ana', '2026-10-01 10:00:00')]; after adding 'a_b' and 'axb', find_users(conn, 'a_b') returns only a_b; add_users(conn, [('hal', T), ('ana', T)]) raises sqlite3.IntegrityError and 'hal' is not stored
edgeCases: Search text containing %, _ or a backslash
Search text in a different case ('AN')
Empty search text; text that matches nothing
A duplicate username in the middle of a batch
hints: Conceptual: a placeholder protects the SQL statement, but inside LIKE the value is still a pattern where % and _ are wildcards. You need a second, different escaping: of the pattern's wildcards, with an escape character you declare in the SQL.

Specific: pick backslash as the escape character with ESCAPE '\' after the LIKE. In the text, replace backslash first (with two backslashes), then % and _ (with a backslash before each); then wrap in % ... % and pass that as the parameter. For User objects, set a row_factory on a cursor, or build User(*row). executemany inside `with conn:` makes the batch one transaction.

Implementation: pattern = '%' + text.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('%', '\\%').replace('_', '\\_') + '%' (in Python source, a backslash in a string is written '\\'); SQL: ... WHERE username LIKE ? ESCAPE '\' ORDER BY username. add_users: with conn: cur = conn.executemany(sql, rows); return cur.rowcount.
evaluation: The backslash is escaped before % and _ (otherwise the added backslashes get doubled)
No SQL text is built from the search text
add_users uses one executemany inside one transaction
